                        One of the requirements to become a citizen in Norway is to pass either the social studies or the citizenship test. The Local has put together some advice on how to best prepare.

The process of acquiring Norwegian citizenship takes years, thanks to the residence requirements, and other conditions such as the language exams, background check, citizenship, or social studies test mean it's a far from straightforward road.

Still, it should be worth it in the end, even if you have to wait a lengthy time to receive a decision on your application due to long processing times.

The main difference between which test you may take will depend on the type of residence you were granted when you first moved to Norway.

The state offers an introduction to Norway programme to some people who move to Norway. This course, usually provided along with language training, aims to get new arrivals up to speed with the country.

Those typically offered these courses originally arrived in Norway on a family immigration or asylum seeker permit.

If you arrived in Norway under the EEA or work permit rules, then you will not have been offered this course.

For those who have done this introductory course, you will likely have been presented with the opportunity to sit the social studies exam. If you have sat and passed this exam in Norwegian, then you are all set, as the exam doesn't have an expiration date and can be submitted with the rest of your documents.

Even if you didn't get the chance to sit this exam in Norwegian or complete the course, fret not, the syllabus for the course will be the same as for the citizenship exam. Therefore, you should have picked up a few things that will be useful for the test.

Most applicants who didn't do the social studies course will probably prefer the citizenship test as it is slightly easier.

The reason it's easier isn't the content of the test itself, as both tests are drawn from the same syllabus. Instead, the language used in the citizenship test is considered more accessible.

Both tests require knowledge of Norwegian history, the school system, healthcare, politics, and geography. They also include questions on societal norms in Norway, working life, and government agencies.

The syllabus is available online and can be divided into the topics of "education skills and the labour market," "family, health and daily life," and "Norway now and before."

These different topics are broken down into various sub-topics. These topics will cover how a system works in Norway and the cultural values behind a particular system – understanding both will give you the tools you need to ace either exam.

Course materials are available in several languages (however, the online portal can be glitchy). The curriculum is found on the website of HK-dir (The Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills).

Thankfully, having the curriculum available should help.

Another helpful aspect of the online curriculum is that it includes discussion points and multiple-choice questions.

For the discussion points, ask somebody to read out the questions to you in English or Norwegian as another way of testing your retention.

There is also an official mock available online. The only downside is that the questions don't change. Still, it should be good for familiarising yourself with how your knowledge will be tested and learning the language used for the test.

There are also unofficial practise exams online. Some of these charge users for access to example questions. Still, there are free mocks available online that applicants can take.

With the right preparation, you should be able to sit the test when you feel ready rather than rushing into it. Local municipalities are responsible for providing the exams and there are quite a few opportunities to take the test throughout the year.

If you need more time to get up to speed with your Norwegian reading skills, or the syllabus then its better to wait a few weeks or couple of months for more slots to open up.

Alternatively, if you want everything ready to submit when you meet the residence requirements, and your Norwegian skills are good enough, then you can take the test ahead of time.

Either way, there's no point in booking a police appointment to hand your documents in until you've passed the test – so there shouldn't be any need to put yourself under any pressure.

articles.title: Skatteetaten: – Har avdekket organisert kriminalitet
articles.content:
Skatteetaten har avdekket feilaktige fradrag på over to milliarder kroner i en av etatens mest alvorlige kontrollsaker på mange år.

Krimsjef Erik Nilsen i Skatteetaten sier til Bergens Tidende at saken fra Bergen er utløst av en større målrettet kontroll som ble varslet i februar.

– I disse kontrollene har vi avdekket omfattende og organisert kriminalitet, og dette er en av Skatteetatens mest alvorlige kontrollsaker på mange år, sier Nilsen til avisen.

De feilaktige fradragene tilsvarer rundt 500 millioner kroner i skattemessig verdi. Avisen skriver at Skatteetaten på landsbasis stiller tilsvarende spørsmål ved likningen til rundt 400 mennesker, de fleste med bakgrunn fra Somalia.

Etaten varsler krav om tilbakebetaling med renter, tilleggsskatt på opptil 60 prosent og politianmeldelser. Så langt er fem saker anmeldt mot tilretteleggere og tolv mot enkeltskattytere.

En mann med somalisk bakgrunn er varetektsfengslet i Bergen, siktet for grovt skattebedrageri som ga 13 personer skattefordeler på over tre millioner kroner.

De 13 personene skal ha overført til sammen 400.000 kroner til mannens konto etter å ha fått utbetalt penger fra Skatteetaten, ifølge Torunn Strand i Vest politidistrikt.

Mannen ble lørdag pågrepet på Flesland lufthavn med enveisbillett til Tyrkia.

– Han erkjenner ikke straffskyld og mener han selv er blitt lurt, sier hans forsvarer Tore Johan Sørland til Bergens Tidende.

articles.content:
Marinen i Oman har reddet 25 sjøfolk fra et tankskip som begynte å brenne etter et angrep. Samtidig melder Iran at tre oljetankere er stanset i Hormuzstredet.  Skipet ble truffet i et angrep som førte til brann om bord. Alle de 25 fikk medisinsk behandling etter evakueringen, men det er ikke opplyst om noen ble skadet. Det er ikke bekreftet om dette er samme skip som Oman har evakuert.

Samtidig hevder Irans revolusjonsgarde at tre oljetankere er stanset etter å ha forsøkt å passere gjennom en skipsled Iran ikke har godkjent.

Iran har begrenset skipstrafikken gjennom Hormuzstredet siden krigen i Midtøsten brøt ut 28. februar.  (NTB)

                        Let's peek behind closed doors at Norwegian bedroom habits.

Given how many internationals move to Norway for love, understanding local intimacy habits can be a practical cultural survival skill, whether you are looking for fresh ideas or simply discovering a shocking reality.

Here are some findings from a survey conducted by YouGov for the adult boutique Nytelse.no that reveal eye-opening insights.

Only 54 percent of Norwegians kiss their partner on a daily basis.

This might come as a surprise to internationals from cultures where showing affection is more common.

If you feel your sex life has slowed down since moving to Norway, you are far from alone. About 59 percent of people have sex once a month or less, and only 36 percent do so weekly. Still, 74 percent wish they had sex at least once a week, and nearly a third want a higher sex drive.

The survey shows that almost one in three women never receive oral sex from their partner, and only 16 percent get it every week.

Friluftsliv may extend beyond hiking in Norway as nearly 8 out of 10 Norwegians (77 percent) would like to have sex outdoors or already do.

Forests are the most popular spot, followed by beaches, lakes, and mountain trails (with Norway's stunning natural landscapes, you won't have any trouble finding a secluded spot)-

More than half of Norwegians (54 percent) masturbate at least once a week. However, there is a big difference between genders: 72 percent of men engage in weekly solo play compared to 40 percent of women.

Only 8 percent of Norwegians rate their love life as a perfect 10 out of 10.

Big tournaments (like the World Cup) often lead to more sexual activity and desire. This is something to keep in mind when planning your calendar around the next big sporting event!

                        PM Støre rejects 'us versus them' approach to immigration in Norway, health minister wants to shake up the healthcare system, getting ready for Halloween, and more news this Friday.

PM Støre rejects 'us versus them' approach to immigration in Norway

​Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre delivered an opening speech at the annual conference of the Directorate of Integration and Diversity (Integrerings- og mangfoldsdirektoratet, or IMDi) in Oslo, declaring that Norway’s growing diversity is now a key part of the country’s identity.

Støre talked about how Norway’s population has changed over the last sixty years, comparing the country he grew up in to today’s society:

"I was born in 1960. You can do the math yourselves, and in the census that year, there were 62,500 foreign-born people living in Norway. That was 1.7 percent of the population. Today, I am 66, and the total immigrant population is over 1.2 million—21.7 percent of the population.

"Out of these 1.2 million, 238,000 are Norwegian-born with an immigrant background, and 340,000 are individuals with a refugee background; that is, from 62,000 to 1.2 million. That is fundamental. And I think one of the most important things, is that this is Norway, and this is who we are. "

Støre emphasised that immigration should not be seen as a contest between the majority and minority groups, referencing King Harald V's iconic 2016  speech on inclusivity:

"The most important thing we must do in our minds is realise that this is not an exercise of 'us versus them'—between a majority population and a minority population—because we are our country. I think King Harald phrased it very well when he said that this is us in Norway, all of us together. We share these tasks together, and we face our challenges together."

You can watch the video of the speech on the website of the newspaper Nettavisen.

Norwegian vocabulary: minoritetsbefolkning - minority population

Date set for renewal of Norway's Norgespris electricity scheme for 2027

The government has announced that households in Norway will need to take action if they want to keep or join the government’s Norgespris electricity scheme next year, as current agreements expire on December 31st and do not renew automatically.

The government introduced the voluntary Norgespris scheme in October 2025 to help households and holiday home owners avoid big changes in electricity prices by offering a steady, subsidised  fixed rate.

To underline the scheme's impact, the government released figures showing in the third quarter (July to September), households saved almost 4.5 billion kroner compared to spot prices, whereas households relying solely on standard electricity subsidies saved under 0.8 billion kroner over the same period.

Analysing its first full year, Norgespris paid out nearly 19.8 billion kroner in support.

"The development of power prices in 2026 shows that Norgespris has been vital. It has given people more predictable electricity bills and security for their wallets," said Energy Minister Terje Aasland in a press statement.

Since the scheme began, the price has stayed at 40 øre per kilowatt-hour (without VAT), however in the 2027 national budget, the government wants to raise the fixed rate to 45 øre per kWh (without VAT). If parliament agrees, this would bring the price to around 56 øre per kWh including VAT starting from the first day of January.

If you want to join the Norgespris scheme next year, you can do so from Tuesday, January 5th, 2027.

Health minister wants the biggest hospital reform in 25 years

Health Minister Jan Christian Vestre has announced that he wants to “shake up” the healthcare system in Norway.

On Monday, an expert committee will deliver recommendations on reorganising hospital governance, which will help him draft a proposal for possible changes, as reported by newspaper Aftenposten.

The committee's goal has been to create a health service that is better connected between hospitals, the municipal health service, GPs, etc., while also considering how to manage the investments and budgets.

​"We have put off many challenges ahead of us for a little too long. Now we actually have to shake things up and think new and different," Vestre told news agency NTB. "I envision the biggest change in 25 years," he added, talking about the current health enterprise model introduced in the early 2000s.

​The current "health enterprise" model split specialist hospital care into four state-owned regional health authorities that are separate from direct political control. Critics say this model is too bureaucratic and puts up barriers between state hospitals and local care services. As a result, vulnerable people, like elderly patients or those with complex mental health and addiction needs, are often moved between disconnected systems.

The minister said he is concerned that patients are sent between different treatments, information is not shared correctly, and follow-ups are missed

He also explained the reform should help patients and front-line healthcare workers rather than administrative structures. The aim is to better connect hospital and local services, so patients get good care no matter who is in charge of it.

The ministry plans to send proposals to parliament and hopes to make the changes before Vestre's term ends in autumn 2029.

Halloween has grown significantly in popularity across Norway over recent decades, so you can expect plenty of people out celebrating across the country on Friday, October 30th and Saturday, October 31st.

In residential neighbourhoods, you’ll see children in costumes going door-to-door for trick-or-treating (knask eller knep in Norwegian), but plenty of adults will also be heading out to themed parties and nightlife events.

If you are making weekend plans, we have listed the best activities in Oslo, Bergen, Stavanger, Trondheim, and Tromsø. The best places to celebrate Halloween in Norway this year

Following the halloween celebrations, November 1st marks All Saints' Day (Allehelgensdag), which in contrast is traditionally a day of reflection in Norway, when people visit cemeteries to light candles on the graves of deceased loved ones.

Thanks to Norway's growing international community,  you will also see global traditions in major cities, like the Mexican Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) events with altars and cultural activities.

Norwegian vocabulary: knask eller knep - trick or treat

"The most important thing we must do in our minds is realise that this is not an exercise of 'us versus them'—between a majority population and a minority population—because we are our country. I think King Harald phrased it very well when he said that this is us in Norway, all of us together. We share these tasks together, and we face our challenges together."

The speech comes during a turbulent period, as immigration is a major topic of debate both in Norway and across Europe.

Friction over integration is particularly evident in current national budget talks, the rising support for the right-wing Progress Party (FrP), whose leader recently called for stricter immigration controls, and an increasingly polarising climate where several politicians with an immigrant background are quitting or considering quitting due to online harassment.

articles.title: Opplysninger om 40.000 ansatte i USAs sikkerhetsdepartement lekket på nettet
articles.content:
En lekkasjenettside har offentliggjort opplysninger om mer enn 40.000 ansatte i USAs sikkerhetsdepartement (DHS), blant dem personer som arbeider med overvåking og etterretning.

Det er organisasjonen Distributed Denial of Secrets som onsdag offentliggjorde opplysningene.

Materialet inneholder navn, telefonnumre, e-postadresser og stillingstitler til ansatte i blant annet immigrasjonspolitiet Ice, grensepolitiet CBP og USAs cybersikkerhetsmyndighet CISA.

Opplysningene avslører også hvilke ansatte som arbeider med spesialoperasjoner, overvåking, dataetterforskning og undercovervirksomhet.

Ifølge organisasjonen stammer opplysningene fra en hackergruppe som kaller seg Department of Peace - Fredsdepartementet.

Gruppen hevder å ha hentet informasjonen fra påloggingstjenesten Okta, som brukes av DHS.

Okta avviser på sin side at deres systemer er kompromittert.

– Okta er sikkert, og vi har ingen bevis for at våre data eller systemer er blitt kompromittert, opplyser selskapet.

Distributed Denial of Secrets sier at opplysningene skal gjøre det lettere for journalister og offentligheten å kontrollere myndighetenes virksomhet.

– Erstatte anonymitet med ansvarlighet, sier medgrunnlegger Emma Best til Reuters om formålet med en søkbar database over de ansatte.

Nyhetsbyrået Reuters har ikke kunnet bekrefte ektheten av hele materialet, men har kontrollert opplysninger om flere ansatte mot andre registre og gjennom direkte kontakt med berørte personer.

Dette er den tredje store lekkasjen av opplysninger om amerikanske statsansatte som er blitt kjent den siste måneden.

I september hevdet hackergruppen ShinyHunters å ha stjålet omfattende opplysninger fra FBI, mens det amerikanske forsvarsdepartementet nylig ble saksøkt etter et datainnbrudd som rammet millioner av nåværende og tidligere militært ansatte.

articles.content:

                        As the leaves turn and the crisp autumn air settles in, Norway's cities come alive with bustling Halloween festivities. We've put together a selection of the spookiest and most entertaining events across the country.

As the air chills and leaves turn, the entire country gears up to celebrate All Saints' Eve, better known as Halloween, on the evening of October 31st (preceding the Christian holiday of All Hallows' Day on November 1st).

In Norway, children celebrate by donning costumes and embarking on a "trick or treat" adventure, knocking on neighbourhood doors with the light on to collect candies, while adults usually opt for Halloween parties and activities.

Whether you're searching for a spine-tingling scare or simply want to embrace the festive autumn spirit, we've compiled a list of must-visit Halloween events in Norway's big cities that will satisfy your Halloween itch.

READ MORE: How Norway adopted the American tradition of Halloween

In Oslo, the celebration begins at the Norwegian Folk Museum, where the Halloween weekend is filled with events that combine spine-chilling themes with rich cultural traditions. Families can choose between Day of the Dead, The Haunted City and The Dark Valley this year.

Deichman libraries are also organising free Halloween activities for children and families across several locations in Oslo. The programme features workshops and drawing challenges, alongside events for adults, including an autumn walk featuring spooky stories.

As Halloween night itself approaches, the Technical Museum transforms into a venue for adult festivities on October 31st. The evening features a Halloween quiz, screenings of classic horror films, VR horror experiences, and an eerie mix of music by DJ Pavlo, ranging from satanic boogie to horror disco.

Until November 1st , Frøya Park at Skarpsno is hosting a Halloween park with decorated tunnels, live horrific characters, circus performers, and light installations.

Oslo's festivities continue with two concerts by the Oslo Symphony Orchestra, with both film and classical music that will put you in the Halloween mood. Organisers encourage attendes to come in their best costume.

TusenFryd, located just 20 kilometres south of Oslo in Vinterbro, is Norway's largest amusement park and has become a beloved Halloween destination over the past few years, though visitors should check availability, as tickets for several time slots are already sold out.

For those seeking adult-themed entertainment, a wide variety of costume and themed parties will be hosted in bars and venues across the city. Just search on Facebook, or their websites.

Bergen's festivities begin with two nights of activities at Mount Fløyen on October 30th and 31st, including a walk through a haunted path, where witches and other spooky creatures can appear when you least expect it.

On October 30th, visitors can enjoy Halloween-themed decor and surprises at the Bergen Aquarium, perfect for a family day out.

The University Museum of Bergen will explore the darker side of nature with family activities, including live blood-sucking insects under microscopes, taxidermy demonstrations, and a hen-mummification workshop.

Additionally, VilVite, Bergen's science centre, caters to families with a special Halloween show and immersive evening experiences.

For party fans aged 20 and over, Social House is hosting the "Garden of Evil" at Teknostallen, featuring guest DJs, visual shows, and a mandatory costume policy.

For those looking for an adrenaline-packed Halloween, a paddle trip along the Nidelva , organised by Tronheimkajakk, invites participants to kayak through a ghostly scene adorned with lights and shadows, offering discounts to those in costume.

Stavanger gears up for what is billed as one of Norway's biggest Halloween parties on October 31st at Fiskepiren.

Fiskepiren, a concert stage and social hub in the heart of Stavanger, will transform into the ultimate Halloween venue. Expect a night of shows and surprises featuring performances by artists like Tom Boye and Doc Lello.

The Stavanger Symphony Orchestra is also bringing some of the most eerie scores in cinema history to life at Stavanger Konserthus on Friday 30th and Saturday 31st .

On Halloween itself, Bjergstedparken will be transformed into a "witch's forest", open to families brave enough to explore - all as part of the Grøss Festival, which runs until November 1st.

Discover the spooky side of the Arctic capital with the 'Mystical Halloween Tromsø' guided walk. Organised by the Troll Museum, the tour explores local myths and legends about ghosts, trolls, huldras and other supernatural creatures from Northern Norway.

Do you know about another Halloween-themed event in Norway which we haven't mentioned? Let us know.

articles.title: The reasons Norway might reject your Norwegian citizenship application
articles.content:

                            There are a number of reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) will reject a citizenship application. Photo by Mark König on Unsplash

                        Norwegian citizenship comes with a hefty application fee and plenty of requirements. There are several reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration might reject an application.

Lifetime enrollment in the Norwegian National Insurance Scheme, the ability to live in Norway for as long as you wish, and returning to Norway after a few years away without going through the immigration process are some of the many benefits of Norwegian citizenship.

Norwegian citizenship doesn’t come easy, though. In addition to waiting years to become eligible, you will have to pass language and citizenship tests, provide a criminal record certificate, verify your identity and meet the requirements for permanent residence if you don’t hold it already.

This is all before you pay 6,500 kroner to apply for Norwegian citizenship.

So, what are the reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) turns down applications?

This applies not just to your citizenship application but also to your entire stay. If you bend the rules when it comes to the residence requirements, you could find your citizenship application rejected.

Even if your application is successful, you will find your citizenship revoked later if the UDI finds out. The UDI will still revoke your citizenship, even if you are the one who decides to come clean to them.

Should the authorities have reason to believe that you have provided incorrect information on any residence or citizenship applications, they will typically invite you for an interview with the police or notify you of your revocation in advance.

READ MORE: How Norway can revoke residency and citizenship over wrong details

This one might seem obvious, but it can happen relatively easily. One of the most common reasons for a foreign national having their citizenship rejected is not passing the citizenship or social studies test (in Norwegian).

For the citizenship test, you must answer 24 out of 36 multiple-choice questions correctly.

The social studies test is taken by those who typically have been through the social studies course for immigrants.

Language-wise, you will generally have to have passed an oral test in Norwegian at  B1 level.

Another common pitfall is the criminal record certificate. Criminal record certificates are only valid for three months. The certification proves that you haven’t been convicted of any crimes and are not disqualified from applying for citizenship.

As the certificate can only be valid for three months, the UDI advises that you shouldn’t order the certificate until you have an appointment to hand in your documents to the police. This reduces the likelihood of the certificate expiring before your documents are handed in.

Failure to meet any of the citizenship requirements will result in your application being turned down. You must also hold a valid residence permit whilst applying for citizenship.

Remember that under standard rules, you must have stayed in Norway for a total of eight of the past eleven years and held residence permits that were each valid for at least one year.

On the UDI website, you can learn how to calculate residence periods in exception cases. However, as there is currently a proposal to amend the Citizenship Act, which could alter how qualifying residence time is measured, these requirements may change in the future.

READ MORE: What will Norway's plan to toughen citizenship rules mean for you?

Being convicted of a criminal offence that results in a fine or prison sentence will bar you from being eligible for citizenship for a set period of time.

The disqualification period can range from 2.5 years up to 39 years, depending on the severity of your punishment. You can see an overview of the disqualification rules on the UDI website.

Those who have received fixed penalty notices rather than criminal fines will not be disqualified. Those who have had charges or cases dropped are also not disqualified.

An example of a fixed penalty notice would be a fine for minor or moderate speeding.

To be eligible for citizenship, you also need to be eligible for permanent residence at the same time, which can make matters confusing.

For many, the easiest way around this is to just hold permanent residence as proof of eligibility while applying for citizenship.

The key thing to look out for when it comes to citizenship is the minimum income requirements for non-EEA permanent residence applicants.

One of the requirements for permanent residence applications for non-EEA nationals is that you will need to have fulfilled the income requirements for the previous 12 months and that you cannot have received financial assistance (økonomisk sosialhjelp) during the prior 12 months.

articles.content:

                        Norway's sovereign wealth fund, the world's largest with assets of more than $2 trillion, on Thursday reported a negative return of 278 billion kroner ($31 billion) in the third quarter as it was weighed down by higher interest rates.

It posted a negative return of 0.5 percent in the quarter, dragged down by a negative return of 3.5 percent in its fixed-income investments, while its equity and property portfolios increased by 0.5 percent and 0.4 percent respectively.

"The fund's return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments," the fund's deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement.

Invested primarily in equities, bonds and real estate across the globe, the fund reported a value of 22,014 billion kroner at the end of September.

Inflation around the world, fuelled in particular by soaring energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East, has led several central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, to raise interest rates in the third quarter.

"Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell," Grande said.

Fuelled by the Nordic country's oil revenues, the fund is invested in more than 7,100 companies spanning the globe, and holds around 1.5 percent of all listed companies worldwide, making it the world's largest single investor.
